Computer science is the study of computation, information, and automation. Computer science spans theoretical disciplines (such as algorithms, theory of computation, and information theory) to applied disciplines (including the design and implementation of hardware and software). Algorithms and data structures are central to computer science. The theory of computation concerns abstract models of computation and general classes of problems that can be solved using them. The fields of cryptography and computer security involve other problems arising from the study of computation.

Abstractions are based on concepts from mathematics, such as algebra, calculus, and discrete mathematics, while software engineering emphasizes practical approaches to software design and development. Computer science is generally considered an area of academic research and distinct from computer programming.

Algorithms and data structures are central to computer science.

Algorithms
An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions used to solve a class of specific problems or to perform a computation. Algorithms are used to specify how to compute outputs from inputs, and they are studied for their efficiency and correctness. Different algorithms may solve the same problem with different trade-offs in speed, accuracy, and memory usage. Algorithms are often expressed in pseudocode, a notation that combines natural language with programming language constructs.

Data structures
A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in a computer so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. Common data structures include arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs. Data structures are chosen based on the requirements of the algorithm and the nature of the data.

Theory of computation
The theory of computation is the branch of computer science that deals with what can be computed and how efficiently it can be computed. It includes the models of computation such as Turing machines and lambda calculus, and the study of computational complexity, which classifies problems into complexity classes such as P, NP, and NP-complete.

Programming languages
Programming languages are formal languages used to communicate instructions to a computer. They provide constructs for defining data, controlling flow, and invoking operations. Programming languages can be classified by paradigm—imperative, functional, logical, or object-oriented—and by level of abstraction—low-level or high-level.

Software engineering
Software engineering is the application of engineering principles to the design, development, testing, and maintenance of software systems. It includes practices such as version control, testing, continuous integration, and agile methodologies.

Computer architecture
Computer architecture describes the organization of hardware components and how they interact to perform computations. It includes the design of CPUs, memory hierarchies, I/O systems, and parallel architectures.

Operating systems
Operating systems are the software that manage computer hardware and software resources and provide services for computer programs. They handle process scheduling, memory management, file systems, and device drivers.

Networks
Computer networks are systems of interconnected computers that communicate and share resources. They rely on protocols such as TCP/IP, HTTP, and DNS to enable communication across local and global scales.

Databases
Databases are organized collections of data stored and accessed electronically. They use query languages such as SQL to retrieve and manipulate data, and they support transactions, indexing, and concurrency control.

Artificial intelligence
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the area of computer science that aims to create systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence. Subfields include machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and robotics.

History
The history of computer science predates the invention of the modern digital computer. Early work in formal logic, combinatorics, and mathematical foundations laid the groundwork for the field. Figures such as Alan Turing, John von Neumann, and Claude Shannon made foundational contributions. The development of the transistor, integrated circuits, and the internet transformed the field and enabled modern computing.

Careers
Computer science graduates pursue careers in software development, data science, cybersecurity, systems administration, research, and academia. The field offers high demand and competitive salaries across industries.
